title: IBM Launches Directed Execution Model and Executor Primitive to Give Researchers Client-Side Control Over QEC Workflows
source_used: IBM Quantum Blog 'Directed execution: Scaling a research platform for quantum error correction' (5 Oct 2026, read via Google News decode); Quantum Computing Report summary (read, 10 Oct 2026)
key_facts: IBM Quantum describes a new lower-level 'directed execution model' for running circuits on IBM Quantum Compute Service hardware.
Error-mitigation steps that used to run as a hidden server-side process now run on the client, where researchers can inspect, customise and extend them.
A new Executor primitive powers the model; it accepts a QuantumProgram and can handle workloads of 5,000 randomisations or more.
The standard Sampler and Estimator tools now run on top of Executor in qiskit-ibm-runtime 0.50.0; IBM says existing code keeps working and in most cases only import statements change.
IBM says the same framework was used for its recent quantum advantage demonstrations with partners.
IBM cites researchers running distance-5 surface codes on its Nighthawk processors with up to 2.8x lower logical error rate per round.
The blog post is dated 5 Oct 2026; Quantum Computing Report summarised it on 10 Oct 2026.
quote_evidence: Directed execution is a new, lower-level execution model that, true to its name, runs your circuits exactly as directed—giving you an explicit, composable way to express how your circuits run and a transparent view into what actually happens on IBM Quantum hardware.
The difference is that the error mitigation they perform is no longer a black box.
For most users, that means the only step you will need to take is updating your provider.
why_it_matters_hint: Researchers working on quantum error handling get visibility and control on IBM hardware; it is a developer tool and the benefits are IBM's own account.
event_date: 5 Oct 2026 (IBM blog post); qiskit-ibm-runtime 0.50.0 released the week before per the post
notes: Quantum Computing Report's page was only readable with compressed transfer; its article is a summary of IBM's blog, so IBM's blog is the source and the link. The item was in our 6 Oct 2026 pool (C15-09, pool only, not in the 6 Oct report). Company claims; no independent test reported.
